content: If blood glucose levels cannot be measured, treat the patient for hypoglycemia. If repeated convulsions occur, administer phenobarbital. If the body temperature is 39°C or higher, provide a dose of paracetamol. Children in shock may present with cold extremities, clammy skin, a weak and rapid pulse, capillary refill time longer than 3 seconds, and low blood pressure. These signs may indicate septicemia, though dehydration can also contribute to hypotension. Correct hypovolemia as needed, take blood for culture, and perform urinalysis. Administer both antimalarial and antibiotic treatments for septicemia. Severe anemia is characterized by severe palmar pallor, often accompanied by a rapid pulse, difficulty breathing, confusion, or restlessness. Immediate blood transfusion is required for children with an EVF ≤ 12% or Hb ≤ 4 g/dL. For less severe anemia (EVF 12–15% or Hb 4–5 g/dL), transfusion is indicated if there is shock, dehydration, impaired consciousness, respiratory acidosis, heart failure, or parasitemia > 20%. Administer 10 mL/kg of packed cells or 20 mL/kg of whole blood over 3–4 hours. Avoid diuretics unless fluid overload occurs. Monitor respiratory and pulse rates every 15 minutes during transfusion. If fluid overload is evident, administer IV furosemide (1–2 mg/kg, up to 20 mg total). Repeat transfusion if Hb remains low, except in severely malnourished children, where only one transfusion of 10 mL/kg whole blood should be given. For hypoglycemia (glucose < 3 mmol/L or < 54 mg/dL), administer 5 mL/kg of 10% glucose solution IV rapidly. If IV access is not possible, use an intraosseous needle or provide sublingual sugar solution. Monitor blood glucose and signs of fluid overload. If fluid overload develops, stop the infusion, repeat 10% glucose (5 mL/kg), and feed the child via a nasogastric tube. Once the child can take food orally, discontinue IV treatment and provide oral or nasogastric feeding. Respiratory distress due to acidosis presents as deep, labored breathing with a clear chest on auscultation, often accompanied by lower chest wall indrawing. It is commonly caused by systemic metabolic acidosis, such as lactic acidosis, and may occur in children with altered consciousness, cerebral malaria, severe anemia, or hypoglycemia. Administer oxygen and correct reversible causes of acidosis, such as dehydration or severe anemia. For Hb ≥ 5 g/dL, give 20 mL/kg of normal saline or Ringer’s lactate IV over 30 minutes. For Hb < 5 g/dL, provide 10 mL/kg of whole blood over 30 minutes, followed by another 10 mL/kg over 1–2 hours without diuretics. Monitor respiratory and pulse rates every 15 minutes. For aspiration pneumonia, position the child on their side or with the head elevated at least 30°. Administer IV ampicillin and gentamicin for 7 days. Monitor the child closely, with nurse checks every 3 hours and doctor evaluations twice daily. Check IV infusion rates hourly and avoid over-infusion. Record fluid intake and output meticulously. Uncomplicated malaria should be treated with a first-line antimalarial agent as per national guidelines. Options include artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) such as artesunate-amodiaquine, artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, or dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine. For P. vivax, a 3-day course of ACT followed by 14 days of primaquine is recommended. For chloroquine-resistant vivax malaria, use amodiaquine, mefloquine, or dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine. In cases of bacterial meningitis, early diagnosis and treatment are critical. Symptoms include fever, seizures, altered consciousness, neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle, and non-blanching petechial rash. Perform a lumbar puncture to confirm the diagnosis and examine CSF. If CSF is cloudy, start treatment immediately. Administer antibiotics such as ceftriaxone (50 mg/kg every 12 hours) or cefotaxime (50 mg/kg every 6 hours) for 7–10 days. In areas with no significant resistance, chloramphenicol plus ampicillin or benzylpenicillin may be used. Review therapy once CSF results are available. Steroids may benefit certain cases of bacterial meningitis (e.g., H. influenzae, pneumococcal, or tuberculous meningitis) by reducing inflammation. Administer dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 2–4 days) within 10–20 minutes before or during antibiotic administration. Avoid steroids in newborns, suspected cerebral malaria, or viral encephalitis. Monitor children with severe conditions closely, especially those with cold extremities, hypoglycemia, respiratory distress, or deep coma. Record any changes in consciousness, behavior, or vital signs. Ensure proper hydration and nutrition, and follow up with outpatient care if necessary.
